At first I kept trying to convince him to give them another chance. “Just wear them for practice.” “Give them a few days.” “You'll get used to them.” Eventually I gave up. I started finding the $400 orthotics sitting in the bottom of his soccer bag instead of inside his shoes. All that money. All those appointments. All that waiting. And they weren't helping anyone sitting underneath a dirty jersey. Then a few months later, I finally convinced him to try them again. He pushed his foot into his shoe... stopped... and looked at me. “Mom, these don't fit anymore.” His feet had grown. Of course they had. He's a kid. I hadn't even really thought about that when we bought them. Then I learned that growing kids may need their orthotics replaced around every six months. So I did the math. $400 twice a year. $800 a year. And he still had years of growing left. By the time my son stopped growing, I could've spent thousands of dollars on custom orthotics. Thousands... on something I still had to argue with him to wear. And customs weren't the only thing we'd tried. Pharmacy insoles. Too flat. Barely any structure. Gel heel inserts. Soft, sure. One in his soccer cleats. One for another pair he wears regularly. title: Don’t make the same mistake I did…
body: I ordered the Footstr InsoleX to fix my kid’s flat feet... And then I panicked. Was my kid going to even like these? What if he wore them once and pulled them straight back out of his cleats? What if this was just another pair of insoles that ended up sitting in the bottom of his soccer bag? I'd been through that before. Custom orthotics were the worst. And not because they didn't work. They actually did. When my son wore them, I could see that his feet weren't rolling inward nearly as much. The problem was everything it took just to get there. First we had to see a specialist. Then the assessment. Measurements. The fitting. Then we waited for them to be made. Then went back again to make sure everything fit properly. Hundreds of dollars later... we finally had these custom orthotics that were supposed to solve the problem. And my son hated wearing them. They were hard. Bulky inside his soccer cleats. He complained that they hurt his feet. At first I kept trying to convince him to give them another chance. “Just wear them for practice.” “Give them a few days.” “You'll get used to them.” Eventually I gave up. I started finding the $400 orthotics sitting in the bottom of his soccer bag instead of inside his shoes. All that money. All those appointments. All that waiting. And they weren't helping anyone sitting underneath a dirty jersey. Then a few months later, I finally convinced him to try them again. He pushed his foot into his shoe... stopped... and looked at me. “Mom, these don't fit anymore.” His feet had grown. Of course they had. He's a kid. I hadn't even really thought about that when we bought them. Then I learned that growing kids may need their orthotics replaced around every six months. So I did the math. $400 twice a year. $800 a year. And he still had years of growing left. By the time my son stopped growing, I could've spent thousands of dollars on custom orthotics. Thousands... on something I still had to argue with him to wear. And customs weren't the only thing we'd tried. Pharmacy insoles. Too flat. Barely any structure. Gel heel inserts. Soft, sure. But they didn't do much for the way his feet rolled inward when he ran. Heel cups. Different shoes. Stretching. Rest. We kept trying things. Some helped a little. Some did basically nothing. But eventually we always seemed to end up in the same place. His feet were still rolling inward when he played. His knees were still bothering him after harder practices. And I was still searching for another answer. So when I saw Footstr... I was interested. But I definitely wasn't convinced. The one thing that made ordering easier was the price. Compared with going through the custom-orthotic nightmare again... Specialist. Fitting. Waiting. Hundreds of dollars. Footstr felt like a pretty small gamble. Still... cheap doesn't matter if your kid won't wear them. So if you just ordered Footstr... Or you're about to order... Let me tell you exactly what happened. Day by day. So you know what to expect. THEY ARRIVED FRIDAY AFTERNOON The first thing I did was take them out of the package and bend them in my hands. They weren't what I expected. The top felt soft. The whole insole had some flex to it. But underneath the arch... there was actual structure. Not that flat piece of foam I'd gotten from pharmacy insoles. And not the rock-hard feeling of my son's custom orthotics either. I bent one again. Flexible. But not floppy. That immediately got my attention. Because that had basically been the problem with everything we'd tried. The comfortable stuff didn't give him enough support. The supportive stuff was so rigid he wouldn't wear it. Footstr looked like it might actually sit somewhere in the middle. But I'd spent enough money getting excited about things in my hands. The real test was getting them onto his feet. FRIDAY EVENING My son was sitting at the kitchen table when I brought over one of his cleats. I'd already taken his old insert out and slipped the Footstr inside. He looked at the shoe. Then at me. “What is it?” “Another insole.” He gave me the look. You know the one. So I told him: “Just try it. If you hate it, take it out.” He pushed his foot inside. Stood up. Walked across the kitchen. Stopped. Walked back. I was waiting for: “No.” Instead he looked down at his feet. Took another few steps. Then shrugged. “These are way softer.” Okay. Good start. But I wasn't celebrating. Walking around our kitchen for thirty seconds is very different from sprinting, cutting and stopping for an entire soccer practice. I'd been fooled by first impressions before. So I went to bed thinking: We'll see tomorrow. SATURDAY — DAY 1 Soccer practice. This was the first real test. Before he ran onto the field I told him: “If they bother you, take them out.” I didn't want him suffering through them because he knew I'd spent money. He nodded. Practice started. Twenty minutes. Still playing. Forty minutes. Still playing. Then the entire session. And I swear I spent half of practice watching his feet. Waiting for him to jog toward the sideline. Waiting for the cleat to come off. Waiting for him to pull the Footstr out and hand it to me. It never happened. He finished practice with them still inside his cleats. When he walked over, I immediately asked: “How were the insoles?” He shrugged. “Fine.” That was it. And weirdly... that was exactly the answer I wanted. I didn't want him obsessing over his insoles. I wanted him thinking about soccer. Still... one practice is one practice. SUNDAY — DAY 2 I put them into his regular sneakers. And then I waited. Normally my son notices everything I put inside his shoes. Too high. Too stiff. Feels weird. Shoe feels tight. This time? Nothing. We went through almost the entire day before I finally asked: “You still have those insoles in?” He looked confused for a second. Then remembered. “Oh. Yeah.” That got my attention. He had basically forgotten about them. TUESDAY — SECOND SOCCER PRACTICE This was the day I was really waiting for. Because almost anything new can survive one wear. The real question is: Will a kid keep wearing it after the novelty disappears? That's where we'd lost the custom orthotics. Again... they worked. When he wore them, his inward rolling looked better. But eventually he started pulling them out before practice. I'd argue. Then bargain. “Just wear them for half the session.” Then I'd find them in the bag anyway. So this time I said nothing. I didn't remind him about Footstr. I didn't ask whether he had put them in. I just watched. Full practice. Still inside his cleats. He came off the field sweaty. Hungry. Exhausted. But he hadn't removed his shoes halfway through practice. He hadn't complained about something hard digging into his foot. He hadn't handed me an insole. They just... stayed in. That sounds small. After everything we'd been through? It wasn't. WEEK 1 — THE FULL PICTURE Before Footstr: $400 custom orthotics. Specialist appointment. Assessment. Measurements. Fitting. Waiting for them to be made. Trying to convince my kid to actually wear them. Eventually finding them sitting in his soccer bag instead of underneath his feet. Then the cheap pharmacy inserts. Easy to wear. But almost completely flat. Gel heel pads. Comfortable... but not the structured support I was looking for. So it felt like there were two choices: Comfortable enough for my kid to wear... but barely any structure. Or: Enough structure... but so rigid he refused to keep them in. After one week with Footstr: He was wearing them. That was the first big difference. Sneakers. School shoes. Soccer cleats. I wasn't arguing with him before practice. I wasn't digging through the bottom of his bag afterward. And for the first time I felt like we'd found the middle ground we'd been missing. Soft enough that my kid would actually wear them. Structured enough to support his arch when his foot started rolling inward. And with cushioning underneath his heel for all the running, jumping and pounding his feet take during sports. WEEK 2 This was when I stopped thinking quite so much about the insoles... and started noticing everything around them. Normally after soccer I could tell how practice had gone before my son even said anything. The way he walked toward the car. How quickly he kicked his shoes off. Whether he started rubbing his knees. Nothing was suddenly perfect. He's still a nine-year-old playing soccer hard. He still gets tired. He still gets sore. But I wasn't seeing the same ritual after every single practice. Just one little thing that used to be part of our routine... that suddenly wasn't happening as often. WEEK 4 — THEN I PULLED THE CUSTOM ORTHOTICS BACK OUT I got curious. Part of me still wondered whether we'd been stupid to abandon something we'd spent so much money on. So I asked my son: “Try your customs again.” He rolled his eyes. Eventually agreed. I put them into his shoes. He pushed his foot down... stopped... and immediately said: “Mom, these don't fit anymore.” At first I thought he just didn't want to wear them. Then I looked. His feet had grown. And that was the moment the economics of this whole thing really hit me. I'd spent around $400 on those orthotics. Specialist. Fitting. Waiting. Getting them adjusted. Convincing him to wear them. Eventually giving up. Then finally getting him to try them again... only to realize he'd already outgrown them. So again I did the math. $400. Twice a year. $800 every year. My son is nine. He has a lot of growing left. By the time his feet stop changing, I could have spent thousands. And I want to say this again because it's important: The custom orthotics did work when he wore them. That's not why I stopped using them. I stopped because the whole process was a nightmare. Appointments. Fittings. Waiting. Hundreds of dollars. A rigid device my kid hated. And then... just when I finally convinced him to give them another chance... his feet were already too big. I did not want to start all over again. That's when Footstr's price stopped looking merely “cheap”... and started looking practical. Four pairs for $30. Instead of hundreds of dollars for one custom device. And four pairs meant I didn't have to move one insole around every day. One pair in his school shoes. One in his sneakers. One in his soccer cleats. One for another pair he wears regularly. That is a completely different decision from: “Do I want to spend another $400 and hope my kid actually wears them this time?” THEN I STARTED LOOKING AT WHY THEY FELT SO DIFFERENT I wanted to understand why he was keeping Footstr inside his shoes when he had fought the customs so hard. There were three things that made sense. 1 - FLEXIBLE ARCH SUPPORT Footstr isn't a completely flat foam pad. There is structure underneath the arch. When the foot starts rolling excessively inward, that support gives the arch something underneath it instead of simply following the collapse. But it still flexes with the foot. Walking. Running. Cutting. Playing. The goal isn't to lock his foot into one rigid shape. It's to give it a steadier base while he's moving. 2 - HEEL CUSHIONING Kids playing sports take an insane amount of repeated impact. Sprint. Stop. Jump. Land. Sprint again. Footstr combines the arch support with cushioning underneath the heel. So there's comfort where the foot lands... and structure where it needs support. 3 - THE STRENGTHENING EXERCISES This was the other big reason I liked them. I didn't want our long-term plan to be: “Put something in his shoe forever and hope.” The insole and the strengthening work have different jobs. The insole supports the arch and heel during the activities that put the most demand on his feet. The exercises give the muscles around his feet something to actually work on outside the shoe. Support during activity. Strengthening work over time. That made much more sense to me. WHY I DON'T WANT TO GO BACK The pharmacy inserts? Easy to wear. Not enough structure for what I wanted. The custom orthotics? Plenty of structure. Expensive. Rigid. A whole specialist process. Quickly outgrown. And most importantly... my kid wouldn't consistently wear them. Footstr landed in the middle. More structure than the flat inserts we'd tried. More flexible than the customs he'd rejected. Cushioning under the heel. Support under the arch. Something he could actually keep inside his cleats while playing soccer. And inexpensive enough that keeping up with a growing kid didn't feel ridiculous. WHAT I WOULD EXPECT IF YOU JUST ORDERED First time they put them on: Don't expect fireworks. Honestly, the best answer might be: “They're comfortable.” Or: “They're fine.” That's a win. You don't want your kid thinking about the thing inside their shoe. First practice: This is the first real test. Cleats tightened. Feet getting hot. Running. Jumping. Cutting. See whether your kid actually keeps them in. That's what mattered most to me. First week: Watch the ordinary things. Are they still wearing them? Are you fighting about them before practice? Are they pulling them out halfway through? What do they say after the activities that normally bring on complaints? Over the next few weeks: Keep your expectations realistic. Footstr isn't going to magically rebuild a growing foot overnight. It's giving the arch and heel support during the activities that demand the most from them... while the strengthening exercises give you something proactive to work on as they grow. IF YOU JUST ORDERED... Don't panic like I did. When I clicked order that Tuesday night, I genuinely wondered whether I'd just bought another pair of insoles my kid would refuse to wear. A few weeks later... I was holding his $400 custom orthotics that he'd already outgrown... while Footstr was still sitting inside his soccer cleats. That comparison pretty much answered the question for me. IF YOU HAVEN'T ORDERED YET... If your kid's feet roll inward... Their feet, heels or knees complain after sports... Or you've already been through the nightmare of expensive custom orthotics they won't consistently wear... Footstr gives you a much simpler place to start. Flexible arch support. Heel cushioning. A strengthening program. And support designed around active, growing feet without locking them against something hard and rigid. Right now, you can get four pairs for $30. So instead of constantly moving one pair between shoes, you can keep them where your kid actually needs them. School shoes. Sneakers. Cleats. Sports shoes. For me? That was a much easier decision than: Another specialist appointment. Another fitting. Another wait. Another $400 custom orthotic. And another argument with my kid about whether he'd actually wear it. Click below to see the Footstr InsoleX 👇

body: I ordered the Footstr InsoleX to fix my kid’s flat feet... And then I panicked. Was my kid going to even like these? What if he wore them once and pulled them straight back out of his cleats? Then the assessment. Measurements. The fitting. Then we waited for them to be made. Then went back again to make sure everything fit properly. Hundreds of dollars later... we finally had these custom orthotics that were supposed to solve the problem. And my son hated wearing them. They were hard. Bulky inside his soccer cleats. I started finding the $400 orthotics sitting in the bottom of his soccer bag instead of inside his shoes. All that money. All those appointments. All that waiting. He pushed his foot into his shoe... stopped... and looked at me. “Mom, these don't fit anymore.” His feet had grown. Of course they had. He's a kid. I hadn't even really thought about that when we bought them. Then I learned that growing kids may need their orthotics replaced around every six months. So I did the math. $400 twice a year. $800 a year. And he still had years of growing left. By the time my son stopped growing, I could've spent thousands of dollars on custom orthotics. Thousands... on something I still had to argue with him to wear. And customs weren't the only thing we'd tried. Pharmacy insoles. Too flat. Barely any structure. Gel heel inserts. Soft, sure. But eventually we always seemed to end up in the same place. His feet were still rolling inward when he played. His knees were still bothering him after harder practices. And I was still searching for another answer. So when I saw Footstr... I was interested. But I definitely wasn't convinced. The one thing that made ordering easier was the price. Trying to convince my kid to actually wear them. Eventually finding them sitting in his soccer bag instead of underneath his feet. Then the cheap pharmacy inserts. Easy to wear. But almost completely flat. Gel heel pads. Comfortable... but not the structured support I was looking for. So it felt like there were two choices: Comfortable enough for my kid to wear... but barely any structure. Or: Enough structure... but so rigid he refused to keep them in. I wasn't digging through the bottom of his bag afterward. And for the first time I felt like we'd found the middle ground we'd been missing. Soft enough that my kid would actually wear them. His feet had grown. And that was the moment the economics of this whole thing really hit me. I'd spent around $400 on those orthotics. Specialist. Fitting. Waiting. Getting them adjusted. Convincing him to wear them. Eventually giving up. Then finally getting him to try them again... only to realize he'd already outgrown them. So again I did the math. $400. Twice a year. $800 every year. My son is nine. He has a lot of growing left. By the time his feet stop changing, I could have spent thousands. title: Every soccer-mom needs to see this ☝️
body: The most overlooked thing about Sever's disease in kids? Everyone treats it like a heel problem. The pain is at the back of the heel. It gets worse during soccer, basketball, running, anything that puts repeated impact through the foot. Some kids start walking on their toes just to avoid putting weight on it. So naturally, the advice is about the heel. Rest it. Ice it. Give him some time. Unfortunately, most doctors tell parents exactly that without ever once looking at how their child's feet actually move. The result? Thousands of parents stuck in the same cycle. Resting, returning, hurting again. Wondering why nothing seems to actually work. My son was one of those kids. He's nine, and for nearly a year Sever's disease had been running our lives. I still remember sitting in Dr. Reeves's office watching him examine my son's heel, press on the back of it, nod, and say: "It's Sever's disease. The growth plate in his heel is irritated. Very common at his age. Give him some rest when it flares up and it'll settle down as he grows." If that sounds familiar, I'm not surprised. Because that's what everyone says. Our doctor said it. Other parents said it. Reddit said it. Every Google result I found at midnight said some version of the exact same thing. And to be fair, rest did work. That was what made the whole thing so frustrating. We would pull him out for a week and the pain would calm down. He'd stop limping. He'd tell me his heel felt fine and practically beg me to let him go back to soccer. Then he'd lace his cleats back up, run onto the field like nothing had ever happened, and within a few practices, sometimes just half a game, we'd be right back where we started. Ice on his heel after dinner. Stretching before bed. Ibuprofen when it got bad. Me lying awake wondering what I was missing while my nine-year-old slept down the hall. I kept telling myself the same thing Dr. Reeves had said: "It'll settle down as he grows." And I wanted to believe that. Honestly, I needed to believe it. Because "he'll grow out of it" meant there wasn't something seriously wrong. It meant I could be patient and eventually this would all stop. Except it wasn't stopping. And the kid who used to wake up on Saturday mornings already wearing his jersey was starting to dread the sport he loved. One night after another rough practice, we were driving home. Normally the ride home is nonstop. He tells me about the shot he almost scored, what his coach said, what some kid did during the scrimmage. Half the time I can't get a word in. That night he didn't say anything. He just sat in the back seat staring out the window. I could see him shifting in his seat, trying to find a position where his heel didn't press against anything. Halfway home he finally said: "Mom... I wanna quit soccer." My stomach dropped. Soccer is his favorite sport in the world. And at nine years old, the pain was bad enough that he was ready to walk away from it. That was the night I decided I was done waiting for him to grow out of anything. The next morning I called a podiatrist. Not another appointment about his heel. I wanted someone who would look at the whole picture. Within ten minutes of watching my son walk barefoot across the office, she stopped him. "Can you stand normally for me?" She crouched down and looked at his feet from behind. Then she looked at me. "Has anyone talked to you about his feet?" Nobody had. Not Dr. Reeves. Not the sports medicine clinic we'd visited once. Not a single person in the year we had been dealing with his heel pain. She pointed to his arches. When he stood with weight on them, they nearly disappeared. His ankles rolled inward. The inside edges of his shoes were visibly more worn than the outside. Then she explained something that changed how I understood the entire problem. The heel is where every step lands. Every sprint, every jump, every landing... the force goes straight through that heel first. When the arch drops and the foot rolls excessively inward, it changes how that impact is absorbed. Instead of spreading more evenly through the foot, the heel takes more of it in a less stable position. And in a growing child, the growth plate in the heel is softer than mature bone. It's more vulnerable to that kind of repeated stress. She referenced a study I later found myself. Researchers looked at school-aged children and found that kids with flat feet scored 42% higher on a clinical pain scale and were significantly less physically active than their peers. She was careful to say that didn't prove his flat feet caused his Sever's disease. But it meant we had been spending a year treating the spot that hurt without ever asking what was happening underneath it every time his foot hit the ground. Then she said the thing that made the entire year click. "Rest calms the irritation on the growth plate. Ice helps with the soreness. But none of that changes how his foot absorbs impact when he goes back to running. So you rest, recover, return, and the same force hits the same heel the same way." I sat there quietly for a minute because suddenly our entire routine made sense. Practice. Pain. Rest. Return. Pain. It wasn't that rest didn't work. It worked every time. It just didn't change what was happening at his feet when he went back to doing the thing he loved. I asked her what we were supposed to do. She said the first step was giving his feet support during the activities placing the most demand on them. Something with cushioning under the heel to soften the repeated impact on the growth plate. Structure underneath the arch to help reduce how far his foot rolled inward. And enough comfort that a nine-year-old would actually keep wearing it. She also said something I hadn't heard from anyone else. Support while he's active is one part of it. But the other part is giving the muscles around his feet and arches actual strengthening work outside the shoe. The long-term goal wasn't for him to depend on something inside his shoe forever. It was to support him now while also working on building stronger movement as he grows. That was the first time in a year that anyone had described an actual plan instead of just telling me to wait. So I started looking. And the first thing we tried was the obvious one. Custom orthotics. Specialist appointment. Assessment. Measurements. Fitting. Then waiting for them to be made. By the time everything was done, we were about $400 in. And to be completely fair, they worked. When my son wore them, I could see that his feet weren't rolling inward nearly as much. The problem was getting him to wear them. He hated how hard they felt underneath his feet. They were bulky inside his soccer cleats. He said they made his shoes feel too tight. At first I pushed him. "Just wear them for practice." "Give them a few days." "You'll get used to them." Then I started finding them at the bottom of his soccer bag, underneath dirty socks and shin guards. $400 worth of support sitting underneath a jersey instead of underneath his feet. Then a few months later I finally convinced him to try them again. He shoved his foot in and immediately pulled it back out. "Mom, these don't fit anymore." His feet had grown. Of course they had. He's nine. So I did the math. $400 every six months or so. $800 a year. And he still had years of growing left. I could have spent thousands on custom orthotics, and I'd still be arguing with him to wear them. That's when I realized there had to be a middle ground. More structure than a flat foam insert from the pharmacy. But more flexible and comfortable than a rigid custom orthotic my kid refused to keep inside his cleats. Support that would actually stay underneath his feet instead of sitting in a bag. And ideally, something paired with the strengthening work the podiatrist had talked about. That's what led me to Footstr. What caught my attention wasn't some promise that it was going to magically fix my son's feet overnight. I'd already spent enough money chasing miracles. It was that Footstr was designed around the exact problem I kept running into: a growing kid who needs support, but still needs to run, jump, cut, and actually tolerate whatever is inside his shoe. And it came with a foot-strengthening program. That was what the podiatrist had described. Support during activity. Strengthening work outside the shoe. Consistency over time. I ordered it that night. When the package arrived, I didn't tell my son I'd found "the answer." I'd made that mistake before. I pulled the old insert out of his cleat, slid the Footstr in, and handed him the shoe. He looked at me. "Another one?" "Just try it." He pushed his foot inside, stood up, and walked around the kitchen. I was waiting for the face. The "nope, take these out" face I'd seen with the customs. Instead he shrugged. "These are way softer." That was it. But after spending $400 on support that ended up in a bag, hearing "way softer" from my nine-year-old felt like a very good start. WEEK 1: The first thing I noticed wasn't his heels. It was that the Footstrs stayed inside his shoes. He wore them to school, then to practice, then to another practice. I didn't have to remind him. I didn't have to argue before games. They just stayed in. That might sound small after everything I've described, but after the custom orthotics, it wasn't. For the first time, the support was actually underneath his feet when he needed it. We also started the strengthening exercises. Nothing complicated. Just a small routine we could realistically keep up with alongside everything else. And for the first time in a year, I didn't feel like our entire plan was "wait for it to get better." WEEK 2: This was when I started noticing what happened after soccer. Normally within minutes of getting into the car he would already be pulling off his cleats and rubbing his heels. Some nights we would already have the ice pack out before dinner. That week he came home from practice and spent half the car ride telling me about a goal he'd almost scored. It wasn't until later that night that I realized something. He hadn't mentioned his heels. Not once. I didn't say anything. I didn't want to jinx it. WEEK 4: By this point the Footstrs had become completely normal to him. School. Soccer. Running around with his friends. He wasn't asking me to take them out and I wasn't checking his bag to make sure they were still there. The strengthening exercises had become part of the routine too. A few minutes here and there instead of another complicated treatment plan we would eventually give up on. Then one night I opened the freezer and noticed something. The ice pack hadn't moved all week. Not because my son had become indestructible. He still got tired and he still got sore sometimes. But the old automatic routine wasn't controlling every week anymore. WEEK 6: We were driving home from soccer. Same route. Same back seat. Same kid looking out the same window. But this time he hadn't been quiet for a single minute. He was telling me about a pass he should have made, a shot that went just wide, and something his teammate said that he thought was the funniest thing in the world. He was talking so fast I could barely follow. And somewhere in the middle of all of it I remembered that drive six weeks earlier. The silence. The shifting in his seat because his heels hurt. The way he barely whispered: "Mom... I wanna quit soccer." Now I was trying to get him to slow down long enough for me to understand what had happened at practice. Soccer felt like soccer again. Not a weekly test of whether his heels could handle it. I don't know exactly what my son's feet will feel like when he's fifteen. Or twenty-five. Nobody does. And I'm not going to tell another parent that a pair of insoles magically fixes every kid. But I spent too long treating "he'll grow out of it" like it meant our only option was to wait. Waiting while he rested. Waiting while his heels hurt. Waiting while the thing he loved slowly became something he was thinking about quitting. Maybe he really would have grown out of every complaint. A lot of childhood aches do improve with time. But after hearing what the podiatrist explained about his feet, and watching the same cycle repeat itself for a year while everyone told me to be patient... "wait and see" stopped being good enough for me. Because when I picture his future now, I don't picture him limping off the field rubbing his heel. I picture him running onto the field without thinking about it. Playing the whole game. Coming home exhausted, muddy, and smiling. Talking my ear off about soccer on the drive home. Maybe one day he decides soccer isn't for him. That's fine. He's nine. He has plenty of time to make that decision. I just never wanted pain to make it for him. Here's what made Footstr different from everything else we tried: 1 - HEEL CUSHIONING This was the biggest one for Sever's. The growth plate in his heel was taking repeated impact every single practice. Sprint, stop, jump, land, sprint again. Footstr cushions underneath the heel so there's a softer landing where his foot takes the most punishment. That alone made a difference I could see. He wasn't pulling his cleats off the second practice ended. 2 - FLEXIBLE ARCH SUPPORT Footstr isn't a flat piece of foam that follows the foot as it collapses. There's actual structure underneath the arch. But it still flexes with walking, running, and playing instead of locking his foot into one rigid position. It gives the arch something supportive to work against while the foot moves naturally. That was the balance I could never find between the floppy pharmacy inserts and the stiff custom orthotics. 3 - FOOT-STRENGTHENING PROGRAM This is what made me feel like we finally had a plan instead of another temporary fix. The insole and the exercises have two different jobs. The insole gives his heel cushioning and his arch support during the activities putting the most demand on his feet. The exercises give the muscles around his feet and arches strengthening work outside the shoe. Support during activity. Strengthening work over time. That was exactly what the podiatrist described, and it was completely different from anything else we had tried. If your child has Sever's disease, their heels hurt after sports, their feet roll inward, or they keep sitting out of the activities they love, it might be worth looking at what's happening at their feet. title: Don’t make the same mistake I did…
body: I ordered the Footstr InsoleX to fix my kid’s flat feet... And then I panicked. Was my kid going to even like these? What if he wore them once and pulled them straight back out of his cleats? What if this was just another pair of insoles that ended up sitting in the bottom of his soccer bag? I'd been through that before. Custom orthotics were the worst. And not because they didn't work. They actually did. When my son wore them, I could see that his feet weren't rolling inward nearly as much. The problem was everything it took just to get there. First we had to see a specialist. Then the assessment. Measurements. The fitting. Then we waited for them to be made. Then went back again to make sure everything fit properly. Hundreds of dollars later... we finally had these custom orthotics that were supposed to solve the problem. And my son hated wearing them. They were hard. Bulky inside his soccer cleats. He complained that they hurt his feet. At first I kept trying to convince him to give them another chance. “Just wear them for practice.” “Give them a few days.” “You'll get used to them.” Eventually I gave up. I started finding the $400 orthotics sitting in the bottom of his soccer bag instead of inside his shoes. All that money. All those appointments. All that waiting. And they weren't helping anyone sitting underneath a dirty jersey. Then a few months later, I finally convinced him to try them again. He pushed his foot into his shoe... stopped... and looked at me. “Mom, these don't fit anymore.” His feet had grown. Of course they had. He's a kid. I hadn't even really thought about that when we bought them. Then I learned that growing kids may need their orthotics replaced around every six months. So I did the math. $400 twice a year. $800 a year. And he still had years of growing left. By the time my son stopped growing, I could've spent thousands of dollars on custom orthotics. Thousands... on something I still had to argue with him to wear. And customs weren't the only thing we'd tried. Pharmacy insoles. Too flat. Barely any structure. Gel heel inserts. Soft, sure. But they didn't do much for the way his feet rolled inward when he ran. Heel cups. Different shoes. Stretching. Rest. We kept trying things. Some helped a little. Some did basically nothing. But eventually we always seemed to end up in the same place. His feet were still rolling inward when he played. His knees were still bothering him after harder practices. And I was still searching for another answer. So when I saw Footstr... I was interested. But I definitely wasn't convinced. The one thing that made ordering easier was the price. Compared with going through the custom-orthotic nightmare again... Specialist. Fitting. Waiting. Hundreds of dollars. Footstr felt like a pretty small gamble. Still... cheap doesn't matter if your kid won't wear them. So if you just ordered Footstr... Or you're about to order... Let me tell you exactly what happened. Day by day. So you know what to expect. THEY ARRIVED FRIDAY AFTERNOON The first thing I did was take them out of the package and bend them in my hands. They weren't what I expected. The top felt soft. The whole insole had some flex to it. But underneath the arch... there was actual structure. Not that flat piece of foam I'd gotten from pharmacy insoles. And not the rock-hard feeling of my son's custom orthotics either. I bent one again. Flexible. But not floppy. That immediately got my attention. Because that had basically been the problem with everything we'd tried. The comfortable stuff didn't give him enough support. The supportive stuff was so rigid he wouldn't wear it. Footstr looked like it might actually sit somewhere in the middle. But I'd spent enough money getting excited about things in my hands. The real test was getting them onto his feet. FRIDAY EVENING My son was sitting at the kitchen table when I brought over one of his cleats. I'd already taken his old insert out and slipped the Footstr inside. He looked at the shoe. Then at me. “What is it?” “Another insole.” He gave me the look. You know the one. So I told him: “Just try it. If you hate it, take it out.” He pushed his foot inside. Stood up. Walked across the kitchen. Stopped. Walked back. I was waiting for: “No.” Instead he looked down at his feet. Took another few steps. Then shrugged. “These are way softer.” Okay. Good start. But I wasn't celebrating. Walking around our kitchen for thirty seconds is very different from sprinting, cutting and stopping for an entire soccer practice. I'd been fooled by first impressions before. So I went to bed thinking: We'll see tomorrow. SATURDAY — DAY 1 Soccer practice. This was the first real test. Before he ran onto the field I told him: “If they bother you, take them out.” I didn't want him suffering through them because he knew I'd spent money. He nodded. Practice started. Twenty minutes. Still playing. Forty minutes. Still playing. Then the entire session. And I swear I spent half of practice watching his feet. Waiting for him to jog toward the sideline. Waiting for the cleat to come off. Waiting for him to pull the Footstr out and hand it to me. It never happened. He finished practice with them still inside his cleats. When he walked over, I immediately asked: “How were the insoles?” He shrugged. “Fine.” That was it. And weirdly... that was exactly the answer I wanted. I didn't want him obsessing over his insoles. I wanted him thinking about soccer. Still... one practice is one practice. SUNDAY — DAY 2 I put them into his regular sneakers. And then I waited. Normally my son notices everything I put inside his shoes. Too high. Too stiff. Feels weird. Shoe feels tight. This time? Nothing. We went through almost the entire day before I finally asked: “You still have those insoles in?” He looked confused for a second. Then remembered. “Oh. Yeah.” That got my attention. He had basically forgotten about them. TUESDAY — SECOND SOCCER PRACTICE This was the day I was really waiting for. Because almost anything new can survive one wear. The real question is: Will a kid keep wearing it after the novelty disappears? That's where we'd lost the custom orthotics. Again... they worked. When he wore them, his inward rolling looked better. But eventually he started pulling them out before practice. I'd argue. Then bargain. “Just wear them for half the session.” Then I'd find them in the bag anyway. So this time I said nothing. I didn't remind him about Footstr. I didn't ask whether he had put them in. I just watched. Full practice. Still inside his cleats. He came off the field sweaty. Hungry. Exhausted. But he hadn't removed his shoes halfway through practice. He hadn't complained about something hard digging into his foot. He hadn't handed me an insole. They just... stayed in. That sounds small. After everything we'd been through? It wasn't. WEEK 1 — THE FULL PICTURE Before Footstr: $400 custom orthotics. Specialist appointment. Assessment. Measurements. Fitting. Waiting for them to be made. Trying to convince my kid to actually wear them. Eventually finding them sitting in his soccer bag instead of underneath his feet. Then the cheap pharmacy inserts. Easy to wear. But almost completely flat. Gel heel pads. Comfortable... but not the structured support I was looking for. So it felt like there were two choices: Comfortable enough for my kid to wear... but barely any structure. Or: Enough structure... but so rigid he refused to keep them in. After one week with Footstr: He was wearing them. That was the first big difference. Sneakers. School shoes. Soccer cleats. I wasn't arguing with him before practice. I wasn't digging through the bottom of his bag afterward. And for the first time I felt like we'd found the middle ground we'd been missing. Soft enough that my kid would actually wear them. Structured enough to support his arch when his foot started rolling inward. And with cushioning underneath his heel for all the running, jumping and pounding his feet take during sports. WEEK 2 This was when I stopped thinking quite so much about the insoles... and started noticing everything around them. Normally after soccer I could tell how practice had gone before my son even said anything. The way he walked toward the car. How quickly he kicked his shoes off. Whether he started rubbing his knees. Nothing was suddenly perfect. He's still a nine-year-old playing soccer hard. He still gets tired. He still gets sore. But I wasn't seeing the same ritual after every single practice. And most importantly... the Footstrs were still in his shoes. Every day. That mattered. Because even the best support in the world can't help much when it's sitting at the bottom of a sports bag. WEEK 3 One night I noticed something strange. The ice pack was still in the freezer. Normally after a hard week of soccer, getting it out had almost become automatic. That week... I hadn't. Not because I'd made some decision to stop using it. I simply hadn't thought about it. Neither had my son. Again... nothing dramatic. No miracle. Just one little thing that used to be part of our routine... that suddenly wasn't happening as often. WEEK 4 — THEN I PULLED THE CUSTOM ORTHOTICS BACK OUT I got curious. Part of me still wondered whether we'd been stupid to abandon something we'd spent so much money on. So I asked my son: “Try your customs again.” He rolled his eyes. Eventually agreed. I put them into his shoes. He pushed his foot down... stopped... and immediately said: “Mom, these don't fit anymore.” At first I thought he just didn't want to wear them. Then I looked. His feet had grown. And that was the moment the economics of this whole thing really hit me. I'd spent around $400 on those orthotics. Specialist. Fitting. Waiting. Getting them adjusted. Convincing him to wear them. Eventually giving up. Then finally getting him to try them again... only to realize he'd already outgrown them. So again I did the math. $400. Twice a year. $800 every year. My son is nine. He has a lot of growing left. By the time his feet stop changing, I could have spent thousands. And I want to say this again because it's important: The custom orthotics did work when he wore them. That's not why I stopped using them. I stopped because the whole process was a nightmare. Appointments. Fittings. Waiting. Hundreds of dollars. A rigid device my kid hated. And then... just when I finally convinced him to give them another chance... his feet were already too big. I did not want to start all over again. That's when Footstr's price stopped looking merely “cheap”... and started looking practical. Four pairs for $30. Instead of hundreds of dollars for one custom device. And four pairs meant I didn't have to move one insole around every day. One pair in his school shoes. One in his sneakers. One in his soccer cleats. One for another pair he wears regularly. That is a completely different decision from: “Do I want to spend another $400 and hope my kid actually wears them this time?” THEN I STARTED LOOKING AT WHY THEY FELT SO DIFFERENT I wanted to understand why he was keeping Footstr inside his shoes when he had fought the customs so hard. There were three things that made sense. 1 - FLEXIBLE ARCH SUPPORT Footstr isn't a completely flat foam pad. There is structure underneath the arch. When the foot starts rolling excessively inward, that support gives the arch something underneath it instead of simply following the collapse. But it still flexes with the foot. Walking. Running. Cutting. Playing. The goal isn't to lock his foot into one rigid shape. It's to give it a steadier base while he's moving. 2 - HEEL CUSHIONING Kids playing sports take an insane amount of repeated impact. Sprint. Stop. Jump. Land. Sprint again. Footstr combines the arch support with cushioning underneath the heel. So there's comfort where the foot lands... and structure where it needs support. 3 - THE STRENGTHENING EXERCISES This was the other big reason I liked them. I didn't want our long-term plan to be: “Put something in his shoe forever and hope.” The insole and the strengthening work have different jobs. The insole supports the arch and heel during the activities that put the most demand on his feet. The exercises give the muscles around his feet something to actually work on outside the shoe. Support during activity. Strengthening work over time. That made much more sense to me. WHY I DON'T WANT TO GO BACK The pharmacy inserts? Easy to wear. Not enough structure for what I wanted. The custom orthotics? Plenty of structure. Expensive. Rigid. A whole specialist process. Quickly outgrown. And most importantly... my kid wouldn't consistently wear them. Footstr landed in the middle. More structure than the flat inserts we'd tried. More flexible than the customs he'd rejected. Cushioning under the heel. Support under the arch. Something he could actually keep inside his cleats while playing soccer. And inexpensive enough that keeping up with a growing kid didn't feel ridiculous. WHAT I WOULD EXPECT IF YOU JUST ORDERED First time they put them on: Don't expect fireworks. Honestly, the best answer might be: “They're comfortable.” Or: “They're fine.” That's a win. You don't want your kid thinking about the thing inside their shoe. First practice: This is the first real test. Cleats tightened. Feet getting hot. Running. Jumping. Cutting. See whether your kid actually keeps them in. That's what mattered most to me. First week: Watch the ordinary things. Are they still wearing them? Are you fighting about them before practice? Are they pulling them out halfway through? What do they say after the activities that normally bring on complaints? Over the next few weeks: Keep your expectations realistic. Footstr isn't going to magically rebuild a growing foot overnight. It's giving the arch and heel support during the activities that demand the most from them... while the strengthening exercises give you something proactive to work on as they grow. IF YOU JUST ORDERED... Don't panic like I did. When I clicked order that Tuesday night, I genuinely wondered whether I'd just bought another pair of insoles my kid would refuse to wear. A few weeks later... I was holding his $400 custom orthotics that he'd already outgrown... while Footstr was still sitting inside his soccer cleats. That comparison pretty much answered the question for me. IF YOU HAVEN'T ORDERED YET... If your kid's feet roll inward... Their feet, heels or knees complain after sports... Or you've already been through the nightmare of expensive custom orthotics they won't consistently wear... Footstr gives you a much simpler place to start. Flexible arch support. Heel cushioning. A strengthening program. And support designed around active, growing feet without locking them against something hard and rigid. Right now, you can get four pairs for $30. So instead of constantly moving one pair between shoes, you can keep them where your kid actually needs them. School shoes. Sneakers. Cleats. Sports shoes. For me? That was a much easier decision than: Another specialist appointment. Another fitting. Another wait. Another $400 custom orthotic. And another argument with my kid about whether he'd actually wear it. Click below to see the Footstr InsoleX 👇 https://getfootstr.com/products/footstr-insolex

title: Don’t make the same mistake I did…
body: I ordered the Footstr InsoleX to fix my kid’s flat feet... And then I panicked. Was my kid going to even like these? What if he wore them once and pulled them straight back out of his cleats? What if this was just another pair of insoles that ended up sitting in the bottom of his soccer bag? I'd been through that before. Custom orthotics were the worst. And not because they didn't work. They actually did. When my son wore them, I could see that his feet weren't rolling inward nearly as much. The problem was everything it took just to get there. First we had to see a specialist. Then the assessment. Measurements. The fitting. Then we waited for them to be made. Then went back again to make sure everything fit properly. Hundreds of dollars later... we finally had these custom orthotics that were supposed to solve the problem. And my son hated wearing them. They were hard. Bulky inside his soccer cleats. He complained that they hurt his feet. At first I kept trying to convince him to give them another chance. “Just wear them for practice.” “Give them a few days.” “You'll get used to them.” Eventually I gave up. I started finding the $400 orthotics sitting in the bottom of his soccer bag instead of inside his shoes. All that money. All those appointments. All that waiting. And they weren't helping anyone sitting underneath a dirty jersey. Then a few months later, I finally convinced him to try them again. He pushed his foot into his shoe... stopped... and looked at me. “Mom, these don't fit anymore.” His feet had grown. Of course they had. He's a kid. I hadn't even really thought about that when we bought them. Then I learned that growing kids may need their orthotics replaced around every six months. So I did the math. $400 twice a year. $800 a year. And he still had years of growing left. By the time my son stopped growing, I could've spent thousands of dollars on custom orthotics. Thousands... on something I still had to argue with him to wear. And customs weren't the only thing we'd tried. Pharmacy insoles. Too flat. Barely any structure. Gel heel inserts. Soft, sure. But they didn't do much for the way his feet rolled inward when he ran. Heel cups. Different shoes. Stretching. Rest. We kept trying things. Some helped a little. Some did basically nothing. But eventually we always seemed to end up in the same place. His feet were still rolling inward when he played. His knees were still bothering him after harder practices. And I was still searching for another answer. So when I saw Footstr... I was interested. But I definitely wasn't convinced. The one thing that made ordering easier was the price. Compared with going through the custom-orthotic nightmare again... Specialist. Fitting. Waiting. Hundreds of dollars. Footstr felt like a pretty small gamble. Still... cheap doesn't matter if your kid won't wear them. So if you just ordered Footstr... Or you're about to order... Let me tell you exactly what happened. Day by day. So you know what to expect. THEY ARRIVED FRIDAY AFTERNOON The first thing I did was take them out of the package and bend them in my hands. They weren't what I expected. The top felt soft. The whole insole had some flex to it. But underneath the arch... there was actual structure. Not that flat piece of foam I'd gotten from pharmacy insoles. And not the rock-hard feeling of my son's custom orthotics either. I bent one again. Flexible. But not floppy. That immediately got my attention. Because that had basically been the problem with everything we'd tried. The comfortable stuff didn't give him enough support. The supportive stuff was so rigid he wouldn't wear it. Footstr looked like it might actually sit somewhere in the middle. But I'd spent enough money getting excited about things in my hands. The real test was getting them onto his feet. FRIDAY EVENING My son was sitting at the kitchen table when I brought over one of his cleats. I'd already taken his old insert out and slipped the Footstr inside. He looked at the shoe. Then at me. “What is it?” “Another insole.” He gave me the look. You know the one. So I told him: “Just try it. If you hate it, take it out.” He pushed his foot inside. Stood up. Walked across the kitchen. Stopped. Walked back. I was waiting for: “No.” Instead he looked down at his feet. Took another few steps. Then shrugged. “These are way softer.” Okay. Good start. But I wasn't celebrating. Walking around our kitchen for thirty seconds is very different from sprinting, cutting and stopping for an entire soccer practice. I'd been fooled by first impressions before. So I went to bed thinking: We'll see tomorrow. SATURDAY — DAY 1 Soccer practice. This was the first real test. Before he ran onto the field I told him: “If they bother you, take them out.” I didn't want him suffering through them because he knew I'd spent money. He nodded. Practice started. Twenty minutes. Still playing. Forty minutes. Still playing. Then the entire session. And I swear I spent half of practice watching his feet. Waiting for him to jog toward the sideline. Waiting for the cleat to come off. Waiting for him to pull the Footstr out and hand it to me. It never happened. He finished practice with them still inside his cleats. When he walked over, I immediately asked: “How were the insoles?” He shrugged. “Fine.” That was it. And weirdly... that was exactly the answer I wanted. I didn't want him obsessing over his insoles. I wanted him thinking about soccer. Still... one practice is one practice. SUNDAY — DAY 2 I put them into his regular sneakers. And then I waited. Normally my son notices everything I put inside his shoes. Too high. Too stiff. Feels weird. Shoe feels tight. This time? Nothing. We went through almost the entire day before I finally asked: “You still have those insoles in?” He looked confused for a second. Then remembered. “Oh. Yeah.” That got my attention. He had basically forgotten about them. TUESDAY — SECOND SOCCER PRACTICE This was the day I was really waiting for. Because almost anything new can survive one wear. The real question is: Will a kid keep wearing it after the novelty disappears? That's where we'd lost the custom orthotics. Again... they worked. When he wore them, his inward rolling looked better. But eventually he started pulling them out before practice. I'd argue. Then bargain. “Just wear them for half the session.” Then I'd find them in the bag anyway. So this time I said nothing. I didn't remind him about Footstr. I didn't ask whether he had put them in. I just watched. Full practice. Still inside his cleats. He came off the field sweaty. Hungry. Exhausted. But he hadn't removed his shoes halfway through practice. He hadn't complained about something hard digging into his foot. He hadn't handed me an insole. They just... stayed in. That sounds small. After everything we'd been through? It wasn't. WEEK 1 — THE FULL PICTURE Before Footstr: $400 custom orthotics. Specialist appointment. Assessment. Measurements. Fitting. Waiting for them to be made. Trying to convince my kid to actually wear them. Eventually finding them sitting in his soccer bag instead of underneath his feet. Then the cheap pharmacy inserts. Easy to wear. But almost completely flat. Gel heel pads. Comfortable... but not the structured support I was looking for. So it felt like there were two choices: Comfortable enough for my kid to wear... but barely any structure. Or: Enough structure... but so rigid he refused to keep them in. After one week with Footstr: He was wearing them. That was the first big difference. Sneakers. School shoes. Soccer cleats. I wasn't arguing with him before practice. I wasn't digging through the bottom of his bag afterward. And for the first time I felt like we'd found the middle ground we'd been missing. Soft enough that my kid would actually wear them. Structured enough to support his arch when his foot started rolling inward. And with cushioning underneath his heel for all the running, jumping and pounding his feet take during sports. WEEK 2 This was when I stopped thinking quite so much about the insoles... and started noticing everything around them. Normally after soccer I could tell how practice had gone before my son even said anything. The way he walked toward the car. How quickly he kicked his shoes off. Whether he started rubbing his knees. Nothing was suddenly perfect. He's still a nine-year-old playing soccer hard. He still gets tired. He still gets sore. But I wasn't seeing the same ritual after every single practice. And most importantly... the Footstrs were still in his shoes. Every day. That mattered. Because even the best support in the world can't help much when it's sitting at the bottom of a sports bag. WEEK 3 One night I noticed something strange. The ice pack was still in the freezer. Normally after a hard week of soccer, getting it out had almost become automatic. That week... I hadn't. Not because I'd made some decision to stop using it. I simply hadn't thought about it. Neither had my son. Again... nothing dramatic. No miracle. Just one little thing that used to be part of our routine... that suddenly wasn't happening as often. WEEK 4 — THEN I PULLED THE CUSTOM ORTHOTICS BACK OUT I got curious. Part of me still wondered whether we'd been stupid to abandon something we'd spent so much money on. So I asked my son: “Try your customs again.” He rolled his eyes. Eventually agreed. I put them into his shoes. He pushed his foot down... stopped... and immediately said: “Mom, these don't fit anymore.” At first I thought he just didn't want to wear them. Then I looked. His feet had grown. And that was the moment the economics of this whole thing really hit me. I'd spent around $400 on those orthotics. Specialist. Fitting. Waiting. Getting them adjusted. Convincing him to wear them. Eventually giving up. Then finally getting him to try them again... only to realize he'd already outgrown them. So again I did the math. $400. Twice a year. $800 every year. My son is nine. He has a lot of growing left. By the time his feet stop changing, I could have spent thousands. And I want to say this again because it's important: The custom orthotics did work when he wore them. That's not why I stopped using them. I stopped because the whole process was a nightmare. Appointments. Fittings. Waiting. Hundreds of dollars. A rigid device my kid hated. And then... just when I finally convinced him to give them another chance... his feet were already too big. I did not want to start all over again. That's when Footstr's price stopped looking merely “cheap”... and started looking practical. Four pairs for $30. Instead of hundreds of dollars for one custom device. And four pairs meant I didn't have to move one insole around every day. One pair in his school shoes. One in his sneakers. One in his soccer cleats. One for another pair he wears regularly. That is a completely different decision from: “Do I want to spend another $400 and hope my kid actually wears them this time?” THEN I STARTED LOOKING AT WHY THEY FELT SO DIFFERENT I wanted to understand why he was keeping Footstr inside his shoes when he had fought the customs so hard. There were three things that made sense. 1 - FLEXIBLE ARCH SUPPORT Footstr isn't a completely flat foam pad. There is structure underneath the arch. When the foot starts rolling excessively inward, that support gives the arch something underneath it instead of simply following the collapse. But it still flexes with the foot. Walking. Running. Cutting. Playing. The goal isn't to lock his foot into one rigid shape. It's to give it a steadier base while he's moving. 2 - HEEL CUSHIONING Kids playing sports take an insane amount of repeated impact. Sprint. Stop. Jump. Land. Sprint again. Footstr combines the arch support with cushioning underneath the heel. So there's comfort where the foot lands... and structure where it needs support. 3 - THE STRENGTHENING EXERCISES This was the other big reason I liked them. I didn't want our long-term plan to be: “Put something in his shoe forever and hope.” The insole and the strengthening work have different jobs. The insole supports the arch and heel during the activities that put the most demand on his feet. The exercises give the muscles around his feet something to actually work on outside the shoe. Support during activity. Strengthening work over time. That made much more sense to me. WHY I DON'T WANT TO GO BACK The pharmacy inserts? Easy to wear. Not enough structure for what I wanted. The custom orthotics? Plenty of structure. Expensive. Rigid. A whole specialist process. Quickly outgrown. And most importantly... my kid wouldn't consistently wear them. Footstr landed in the middle. More structure than the flat inserts we'd tried. More flexible than the customs he'd rejected. Cushioning under the heel. Support under the arch. Something he could actually keep inside his cleats while playing soccer. And inexpensive enough that keeping up with a growing kid didn't feel ridiculous. WHAT I WOULD EXPECT IF YOU JUST ORDERED First time they put them on: Don't expect fireworks. Honestly, the best answer might be: “They're comfortable.” Or: “They're fine.” That's a win. You don't want your kid thinking about the thing inside their shoe. First practice: This is the first real test. Cleats tightened. Feet getting hot. Running. Jumping. Cutting. See whether your kid actually keeps them in. That's what mattered most to me. First week: Watch the ordinary things. Are they still wearing them? Are you fighting about them before practice? Are they pulling them out halfway through? What do they say after the activities that normally bring on complaints? Over the next few weeks: Keep your expectations realistic. Footstr isn't going to magically rebuild a growing foot overnight. It's giving the arch and heel support during the activities that demand the most from them... while the strengthening exercises give you something proactive to work on as they grow. IF YOU JUST ORDERED... Don't panic like I did. When I clicked order that Tuesday night, I genuinely wondered whether I'd just bought another pair of insoles my kid would refuse to wear. A few weeks later... I was holding his $400 custom orthotics that he'd already outgrown... while Footstr was still sitting inside his soccer cleats. That comparison pretty much answered the question for me. IF YOU HAVEN'T ORDERED YET... If your kid's feet roll inward... Their feet, heels or knees complain after sports... You do not say anything. Neither do they. But you are both thinking the same thing. Falls. One in four adults over 65 falls every year. Not from the inner ear alone. Not from vision alone. From the feet reading the ground and sending constant feedback upward so the brain can make micro-adjustments thousands of times per day. Thick cushioned shoes cut that signal at the source. Your parents are walking blind from the ankles down. Then there are their toes. They cannot do the one thing toes were designed to do — create five independent contact points that stabilize the foot on every surface. Five toes gripping independently is the difference between a hand pressing flat on a table and a hand gripping the edge of it. One slides. One holds. Your parents' toes have not gripped a surface in years. Their shoes will not let them. And then there is the heel. Every cushioned shoe has a raised heel. That raised heel forces the foot to reach forward with every step, landing ahead of the body and creating a braking force on every single step. On dry flat ground, this is uncomfortable but manageable. On a wet porch, a smooth tile, or an uneven sidewalk, that forward-reaching braking heel is a fall waiting to happen. So your parents are walking with feet that cannot feel the ground, toes that cannot grip, and a heel that brakes instead of rolls. And you bought them those shoes thinking you were helping. She fell again six weeks later. In the kitchen. On dry tile. In those shoes. That is when I started asking different questions. Not which shoes have more support. But why her feet stopped supporting her. The answer was the shoes themselves. Decades of thick soles had shut down the nerve endings in her feet. Years of narrow toe boxes had compressed her toes into one useless block. The muscles across the bottom of each foot had weakened because the shoes were doing all the work. Her feet were not aging. The first thing she said was she could feel the kitchen tile under her feet again. Not painful. Just present. She knew where the floor was in a way she had not known in years. By the end of the first week she stopped holding the counter when she walked to the sink. By week two her toes were visibly spreading when she stood. Not from exercises. From finally having room to do what they were designed to do. By week four she walked the garden path out back without looking down once. The same path I had been quietly terrified of for three years. Her feet woke up. The five toe pockets let each toe grip the ground independently. The zero-drop sole let her foot land beneath her body instead of reaching forward. The carved pressure-mapped sole stimulated nerve endings that had been dormant under foam for decades. And the thin Dyneema construction protected her from sharp surfaces while keeping her close enough to the ground to feel every surface change. Her balance did not improve because she got younger. It improved because her feet started receiving information and responding to it again. Your parents do not need more cushioning. They need their feet back. SuperSocks give them five toes that grip. A sole that talks to their brain. And the protection to wear them on every surface in and around their home. Click below to grab a pair for your parents before the next wet morning.

title: Neuropathy did not kill your nerves. It starved them. This sole feeds them again.
body: Here is something nobody tells you about neuropathy. Your nerves are not all dead. Most of them are still there. Still connected. Still capable of firing. They are starving. A nerve ending that receives no stimulation does not fire. A nerve ending that does not fire begins to go dormant. A nerve ending that stays dormant long enough starts to feel dead even when it is not. Now look at what is under your feet right now. A flat sole. Smooth. Featureless. One uniform surface sending one uniform signal across thousands of nerve endings. The same monotone input from heel to toe. No variation. No texture. No pressure differences. Nothing for any individual nerve to differentiate or respond to. Your nerves are not dying from neuropathy alone. They are dying from neuropathy plus a sole that gives them absolutely nothing to hold on to. One man said he had not felt the floor in years. Not the cold of tile. Not the grain of wood. Not the texture of carpet. Just a vague dull pressure that told him something was down there but not what. He said walking felt like walking on blocks of wood strapped to the ends of his legs. Another said the scariest part was not the numbness. It was the falling. He could not feel the edge of a curb. He could not feel the transition from sidewalk to grass. He could not feel whether his foot was fully on the step or half off it. His eyes did everything. His feet told him nothing. Another said he had started holding furniture when he walked through his own house. Not because his legs were weak. Because his feet could not confirm where the floor was. These men do not have a balance problem. They do not have a leg problem. They have feet that are receiving zero information from the ground and a brain that cannot stabilize what it cannot feel. Here is what nobody in their doctor's office is talking about. The nerve endings in the sole of the human foot are mechanoreceptors. They fire in response to mechanical pressure. Texture. Contour. Variation. They evolved on surfaces that were never flat. Roots. Stones. Packed earth. Sand. Bark. Uneven terrain that pressed into the sole differently at every point with every step. Thousands of nerve endings receiving thousands of distinct signals simultaneously. That is the input that kept them alive. That is the input that kept them firing. That is the input that your flat smooth modern sole deleted. You would not expect your eyes to stay sharp in a pitch black room. You would not expect your ears to stay sharp in total silence. So why would you expect nerve endings in the sole of your foot to stay active when the only surface they ever touch is a flat featureless slab of foam? Neuropathy damages nerves from the inside. Your sole starves them from the outside. You are fighting on two fronts and only treating one. SuperSocks Wood Carved Edition does not treat neuropathy. It addresses the front nobody is talking about. The sole. ✔ Patented Wood-Carved Anatomical Sole. Not flat. Not smooth. Not one signal. Carved. Three distinct pressure zones each with a different textured pattern mapped to a different region of the plantar surface. The heel zone has one carved contour that presses a specific pattern into the heel pad. The midfoot zone has a different carved contour that presses into the arch. The forefoot zone has a third pattern that presses into the ball of the foot and the base of each toe. Every step delivers hundreds of distinct pressure points across the sole. Not one monotone signal. A complex textured conversation between the sole and every nerve ending that is still capable of responding. You are not treating the nerves. You are giving them a reason to fire again. And the ones that can fire will ✔ Five-Toe Separation. Each toe sits in its own individual channel with its own section of carved texture beneath the pad. That means five independent nerve stimulation zones at the tips of your feet where neuropathy hits first and hardest. Instead of five toes compressed together receiving one shared signal, each toe gets its own distinct input. The nerve endings in your big toe pad get a different carved texture than the nerve endings in your second toe pad. Each toe becomes an independent sensory checkpoint. The first thing most people feel coming back is their big toe. Then the second. Then the others. One by one. Channel by channel. Because each one is finally receiving its own signal instead of sharing one ✔ Zero Drop. Heel and forefoot on the same level. No raised heel tilting your weight forward onto numb toes that cannot feel where they are landing. Your weight distributes across the full sole instead of concentrating on the forefoot where sensation is weakest. Every nerve ending across all three zones shares the load and shares the stimulation ✔ 15X Stronger Than Steel. Dyneema protection handles glass sharp gravel and rough surfaces. Everything dangerous gets blocked. But the textured pressure signals from the carved sole get through fully. You do not need to feel pain to feel the ground. You need to feel texture and pressure and variation. The carved sole delivers that. The Dyneema blocks everything else ✔ 3,000+ NanoGrip Fusion Points. When your feet cannot feel the ground your fall risk goes through the roof on wet or smooth surfaces. NanoGrip holds on surfaces where your eyes cannot help you — wet tile, smooth concrete, rainy sidewalks. Grip that does not depend on sensation ✔ 10X More Durable. He said it was like his heel remembered what the ground was. Another said after two weeks he could feel the difference between standing on his kitchen tile and standing on the carpet in his living room. He had not felt a floor transition in years. He stood in the doorway between the two rooms and cried. Another said his balance changed before his sensation fully returned. Not because he could feel the ground yet. Because the carved texture was giving his brain just enough information to stabilize even before the nerves fully woke up. title: Rome Built the Feet Before the Fighter 🏛️
body: Before he ruled Rome, he marched. Twenty miles in five hours, in leather straps and a thin flat sole. Every Roman soldier did it before he ever touched a sword. Rome built the feet before the fighter. A sole that thin lets the foot work. Toes grip. Arch loads like a spring. Every step made his feet stronger, and everything above them followed. Then in the 1970s, shoes went soft. Cushion lifted your heel, cut your feet off from the ground, and handed the work to your knees and back. That's where the pain began… We brought the caliga back. Without the shoe. Introducing SuperSocks WoodCarved 2.0. The one and only sock on the market with a patented sole, hand-sewn to your exact pressure points to reactivate your foot muscles. We asked foot biomechanists one question: where does a bare foot actually touch the ground? The ball. The heel. Under each toe. Then we took full-grain cowhide, real leather like the caliga, and hand-stitched a wood-carved section onto every one of those points, so: ✅ Each section lands on the exact spot, every step, and the muscle under it has to fire ✅ Nothing under the arch, so it flexes like a spring and gets strong on its own ✅ Knees, hips and back stop doing your feet's job Not glued. Stitched. It doesn't slip, it doesn't shift. Full-grain is the top layer of the hide, nothing sanded off, so the section that works hardest doesn't wear through. title: Best Shoes for Plantar Fasciitis
body: If you've got plantar fasciitis, stop wearing shoes that fold in half. Soft and bendy feels comfortable in the shop... but it overloads your arch all day. Here are the 5 features I look for when helping patients recover: 1️⃣ Firm heel counter You want the back of the shoe to feel solid. This limits excessive pronation and keeps the ankle stable. 2️⃣ Deep, supportive heel cup It should wrap around your heel bone and spread pressure evenly. This reduces strain through the inside of the heel. @kurufootwear builds this directly into the shoe with their curved heel technology, so you can actually feel that medial heel support. 3️⃣ Higher heel to toe drop A thicker heel compared to the forefoot reduces strain on your calf, arch, and plantar fascia. 4️⃣ Stiffness through the midfoot If you can easily twist or fold the shoe, it is too soft. A firmer shoe gives your foot the stability it needs while healing. 5️⃣ Slight rocker This helps roll you forward so you are not overloading your big toe and arch with every step. The right shoe will not cure plantar fasciitis overnight... but the wrong shoe will slow your recovery down. Check out @kurufootwear's range of shoes. #ad

Then one night while scrolling online, I came across people talking about ankle compression socks. At first, I didn’t understand how something smaller and lighter could actually help, but person after person kept saying the same thing. They didn’t need heavy knee-high compression to feel relief. The gentle support around the feet and ankles was enough. That’s how I found Viasox Ankle Compression Socks. The first thing I noticed was how comfortable they felt. No squeezing around my calves. No struggling to pull them on. Just light, supportive compression exactly where my feet needed it most. I started wearing them while traveling, during long days on my feet, and even around the house. After a couple of weeks, my feet felt lighter, less swollen, and much less fatigued at the end of the day. Even the burning and tingling I used to notice constantly felt less distracting. What surprised me most was how much easier ankle compression felt compared to traditional compression socks. They were breathable, lightweight, and actually realistic to wear every day. Now I wear them all the time because my feet simply feel better when I do. So if you’ve been struggling with swollen feet, aching ankles, neuropathy discomfort, or tired heavy feet, maybe you don’t need thicker compression. Maybe you just need the right kind. Try Viasox Ankle Compression Socks and feel the difference for yourself.

title: Neuropathy Pain? Start Here!
body: Living with diabetes and neuropathy meant my feet were extra sensitive. By the end of the day, I’d peel my socks off and see those deep red rings around my calves. My feet would feel hot, tender, and irritated, and the seams near my toes always seemed to rub in exactly the wrong place. When you have diabetes or neuropathy, little things don’t feel little. A tight band, a rough seam, or a thin sole can make the whole day harder. Then I tried Viasox EasyStretch™ Socks. The first thing I noticed was how easy they were to put on. No tugging. No fighting to get them over swollen feet. They stretched without squeezing, and the non-binding top actually stayed up without digging into my legs. Then I felt the cushioning. The triple-padded heel and toe gave my feet the softness regular socks never did. And the seamless toe? No rubbing. No irritation. Just smooth comfort. Now I can wear socks all day without constantly thinking about my feet. No deep marks. No tight elastic. No painful seams. Just soft, breathable comfort that finally feels made for sensitive, diabetic, and neuropathy-prone feet. If diabetes or neuropathy has made regular socks unbearable, Viasox EasyStretch™ Socks are worth trying.
